claim: Foldback inversions have been observed in human genetic diseases and cancers.
source: Foldback inversions, also called inverted duplications, have been observed in human genetic diseases and cancers.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established observations in the literature about foldback inversions in human diseases.

claim: Foldback inversions were mediated by formation of single-stranded DNA hairpins.
source: Foldback inversions were mediated by formation of single-stranded DNA hairpins.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two types of hairpins were identified: small-loop hairpins and large-loop hairpins.
source: Two types of hairpins were identified: small-loop hairpins that were suppressed by MRE11, SAE2, SLX1, and YKU80 and large-loop hairpins that were suppressed by YEN1, TEL1, SWR1, and MRC1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 5-9.

claim: Small-loop hairpins were suppressed by MRE11, SAE2, SLX1, and YKU80.
source: Two types of hairpins were identified: small-loop hairpins that were suppressed by MRE11, SAE2, SLX1, and YKU80 and large-loop hairpins that were suppressed by YEN1, TEL1, SWR1, and MRC1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 7, and 8.

claim: Large-loop hairpins were suppressed by YEN1, TEL1, SWR1, and MRC1.
source: Two types of hairpins were identified: small-loop hairpins that were suppressed by MRE11, SAE2, SLX1, and YKU80 and large-loop hairpins that were suppressed by YEN1, TEL1, SWR1, and MRC1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data from previous studies and current analysis in Figures 5-8.

claim: Long-stem hairpin-forming sequences could form foldback inversions when proximal or distal to the DSB.
source: Analysis of CRISPR/Cas9-induced double strand breaks (DSBs) revealed that long-stem hairpin-forming sequences could form foldback inversions when proximal or distal to the DSB, whereas short-stem hairpin-forming sequences formed foldback inversions when proximal to the DSB.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Short-stem hairpin-forming sequences formed foldback inversions when proximal to the DSB.
source: Analysis of CRISPR/Cas9-induced double strand breaks (DSBs) revealed that long-stem hairpin-forming sequences could form foldback inversions when proximal or distal to the DSB, whereas short-stem hairpin-forming sequences formed foldback inversions when proximal to the DSB.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Foldback inversion GCRs were stabilized by secondary rearrangements, mostly mediated by different homologous recombination mechanisms including single-strand annealing.
source: Finally, we found that foldback inversion GCRs were stabilized by secondary rearrangements, mostly mediated by different homologous recombination mechanisms including single-strand annealing; however, POL32-dependent break-induced replication did not appear to be involved forming secondary rearrangements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 6-9 and analysis of GCR structures.

claim: POL32-dependent break-induced replication did not appear to be involved in forming secondary rearrangements.
source: Finally, we found that foldback inversion GCRs were stabilized by secondary rearrangements, mostly mediated by different homologous recombination mechanisms including single-strand annealing; however, POL32-dependent break-induced replication did not appear to be involved forming secondary rearrangements.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 9 showing that pol32Δ mutants still form foldback inversions with secondary rearrangements.

claim: Characteristic GCRs underlie many human diseases, including leukemias and lymphomas.
source: Characteristic GCRs underlie many human diseases, including leukemias and lymphomas (Mitelman et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mitelman et al., 2007.

claim: Ongoing accumulation of mutations and GCRs is seen in many types of cancer.
source: In addition, ongoing accumulation of mutations and GCRs is seen in many types of cancer (Campbell et al., 2010; Gibson et al., 2016; Gundem et al., 2015; Nowell, 1976; Uchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: RAD27 encodes a flap endonuclease involved in Okazaki fragment maturation.
source: Many of the genes identified in these studies can be characterized as having important roles in (1) preventing the accumulation of DNA damage (e.g. RAD27, which encodes a flap endonuclease involved in Okazaki fragment maturation [Kao and Bambara, 2003])
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kao and Bambara, 2003.

claim: RAD52 encodes a protein involved in loading the Rad51 strand-exchange protein.
source: (2) promoting the repair of DNA damage through conservative repair mechanisms, such as allelic homologous recombination (HR) (e.g. RAD52, which encodes a protein involved in loading the Rad51 strand-exchange protein [Krogh and Symington, 2004])
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Krogh and Symington, 2004.

claim: PIF1 encodes a DNA helicase that suppresses de novo telomere addition to double-strand breaks.
source: (3) preventing the aberrant repair of DNA damage, which can act on intermediates that are normally processed by conservative repair pathways (e.g. PIF1, which encodes a DNA helicase that suppresses de novo telomere addition to double-strand breaks (DSBs) [Myung et al., 2001; Schulz and Zakian, 1994]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Myung et al., 2001 and Schulz and Zakian, 1994.

claim: Foldback inversions have been observed in pancreatic, ovarian, breast and esophageal cancer.
source: These types of inversions have been observed in human cancers, including pancreatic, ovarian, breast and esophageal cancer, are associated with poor prognosis in high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and occur in syndromes underlying autism, birth defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (Ballif et al., 2003; Bonaglia et al., 2009; Campbell et al., 2010; Ford and Fried, 1986; Guenthoer et al., 2012; Hermetz et al., 2014; Stephens et al., 2009; Tanaka et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017b; Yu and Graf, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to cancer genomics studies.

claim: Foldback inversions are associated with poor prognosis in high-grade serous ovarian cancer.
source: These types of inversions have been observed in human cancers, including pancreatic, ovarian, breast and esophageal cancer, are associated with poor prognosis in high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and occur in syndromes underlying autism, birth defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (Ballif et al., 2003; Bonaglia et al., 2009; Campbell et al., 2010; Ford and Fried, 1986; Guenthoer et al., 2012; Hermetz et al., 2014; Stephens et al., 2009; Tanaka et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017b; Yu and Graf, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations including Campbell et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2017b.

claim: Foldback inversions occur in syndromes underlying autism, birth defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability.
source: These types of inversions have been observed in human cancers, including pancreatic, ovarian, breast and esophageal cancer, are associated with poor prognosis in high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and occur in syndromes underlying autism, birth defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability (Ballif et al., 2003; Bonaglia et al., 2009; Campbell et al., 2010; Ford and Fried, 1986; Guenthoer et al., 2012; Hermetz et al., 2014; Stephens et al., 2009; Tanaka et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017b; Yu and Graf, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to genetic disease studies.

claim: Some engineered palindromic inversions are unstable and are cleaved by the Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2 complex and Sae2.
source: Interestingly, some engineered palindromic inversions are unstable, are cleaved by the Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2 complex and Sae2 and induce GCRs (Lobachev et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lobachev et al., 2002.

claim: The sae2Δ mutation caused increases in the uGCR rate.
source: Consistent with previous reports that the Sae2-S267A and Sae2-MT9 proteins are defective for Sae2 function (Baroni et al., 2004; Huertas et al., 2008), the sae2Δ, sae2-S267A, and sae2-MT9 mutations caused equivalent increases in the uGCR rate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The sae2-S267A mutation caused increases in the uGCR rate equivalent to sae2Δ.
source: Consistent with previous reports that the Sae2-S267A and Sae2-MT9 proteins are defective for Sae2 function (Baroni et al., 2004; Huertas et al., 2008), the sae2Δ, sae2-S267A, and sae2-MT9 mutations caused equivalent increases in the uGCR rate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1, and citations to Baroni et al., 2004 and Huertas et al., 2008.

claim: The sae2-MT9 mutation caused increases in the uGCR rate equivalent to sae2Δ.
source: Consistent with previous reports that the Sae2-S267A and Sae2-MT9 proteins are defective for Sae2 function (Baroni et al., 2004; Huertas et al., 2008), the sae2Δ, sae2-S267A, and sae2-MT9 mutations caused equivalent increases in the uGCR rate.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1, and citations to Baroni et al., 2004 and Huertas et al., 2008.

claim: The mre11Δ mutation caused higher GCR rates than sae2 mutations.
source: However, these GCR rates were lower than those caused by mre11Δ mutation and mre11-H125N mutation, the latter of which eliminates the Mre11 nuclease activity (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1; Liang et al., 2018; Putnam et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1, and citations to Liang et al., 2018 and Putnam et al., 2009.

claim: The mre11-H125N mutation eliminates the Mre11 nuclease activity.
source: However, these GCR rates were lower than those caused by mre11Δ mutation and mre11-H125N mutation, the latter of which eliminates the Mre11 nuclease activity (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1; Liang et al., 2018; Putnam et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2018 and Putnam et al., 2009.

claim: In sae2Δ mutants, 19 of 20 GCRs were foldback inversions.
source: In almost all cases (sae2Δ: 19 of 20 GCRs. sae2-S267A: 12 of 12 GCRs. sae2-MT9: 11 of 12 GCRs), WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In sae2-S267A mutants, 12 of 12 GCRs were foldback inversions.
source: In almost all cases (sae2Δ: 19 of 20 GCRs. sae2-S267A: 12 of 12 GCRs. sae2-MT9: 11 of 12 GCRs), WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In sae2-MT9 mutants, 11 of 12 GCRs were foldback inversions.
source: In almost all cases (sae2Δ: 19 of 20 GCRs. sae2-S267A: 12 of 12 GCRs. sae2-MT9: 11 of 12 GCRs), WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Foldback inversion GCRs contain a deletion that spanned some or all of the counter-selected CAN1/URA3 cassette.
source: WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L (Figure 1D,E; Supplementary file 3): (1) a deletion that spanned some or all of the counter-selected CAN1/URA3 cassette
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and read depth plots shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Foldback inversion GCRs contain a duplication that extended from the deletion to a more centromeric site.
source: WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L (Figure 1D,E; Supplementary file 3): (1) a deletion that spanned some or all of the counter-selected CAN1/URA3 cassette; (2) a duplication that extended from the deletion to a more centromeric site
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and read depth plots shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Foldback inversion GCRs contain discordant read pairs that indicated a novel inversion junction at the telomeric side of the duplication.
source: WGS revealed features of a foldback inversion GCR on chrV L (Figure 1D,E; Supplementary file 3): (1) a deletion that spanned some or all of the counter-selected CAN1/URA3 cassette; (2) a duplication that extended from the deletion to a more centromeric site; (3) discordant read pairs that indicated a novel inversion junction at the telomeric side of the duplication
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data and read depth plots shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: sae2 mutations caused increases in the rate of accumulating foldback inversions that were ~240 fold higher than that of the wild-type strain.
source: Using the GCR rates and GCR spectra obtained, we found that sae2 mutations caused increases in the rate of accumulating foldback inversions that were ~240 fold higher than that of the wild-type strain (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: mre11 mutations caused higher rates of accumulating foldback inversions than sae2 mutations.
source: In contrast, mre11 mutations caused higher rates of accumulating foldback inversions than sae2 mutations; however, this difference was less than the difference in total GCR rates observed for mre11 and sae2 mutants (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Mutations in SAE2 almost exclusively caused the formation of foldback inversions (92–100% of the GCRs).
source: Mutations in SAE2 almost exclusively caused the formation of foldback inversions (92–100% of the GCRs), whereas mre11 mutants accumulated a diversity of GCRs including foldback inversions (30–50% of the GCRs; Supplementary file 1; Chen and Kolodner, 1999; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and citations to Chen and Kolodner, 1999 and Liang et al., 2018.

claim: mre11 mutants accumulated a diversity of GCRs including foldback inversions (30–50% of the GCRs).
source: Mutations in SAE2 almost exclusively caused the formation of foldback inversions (92–100% of the GCRs), whereas mre11 mutants accumulated a diversity of GCRs including foldback inversions (30–50% of the GCRs; Supplementary file 1; Chen and Kolodner, 1999; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and citations to Chen and Kolodner, 1999 and Liang et al., 2018.

claim: The Sae2-Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2 endonuclease is a known substrate for ssDNA hairpins.
source: A mechanism for forming a foldback inversion consistent with this intermediate involves: (1) 5'-resection from a DSB or other initiating damage, exposing inverted ssDNA sequences; (2) formation of a ssDNA hairpin intermediate, which is a known substrate for the Sae2-Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2 endonuclease (Oh and Symington, 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Oh and Symington, 2018.

claim: Most foldback inversion GCRs isolated in mre11-H125N, sae2Δ, sae2-S267A, and sae2-MT9 single mutant strains were mediated by an inversion hotspot sequence in the can1::hisG disruption cassette.
source: Most foldback inversion GCRs isolated in mre11-H125N, sae2Δ, sae2-S267A, and sae2-MT9 single mutant strains, as well as the sae2Δ double mutant strains described below, were mediated by an inversion hotspot sequence in the can1::hisG disruption cassette within the GCR assay breakpoint region (coordinates chrV 34,339–107_34,339–75; Figure 3A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The inversion hotspot is predicted to form a ssDNA hairpin with a 3 nt loop and a 15 bp stem.
source: This hotspot, when present in ssDNA, is predicted to form a ssDNA hairpin with a 3 nt loop and a 15 bp stem (Figure 3B), which is the longest stem available for ssDNA hairpins in the uGCR assay breakpoint region (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural prediction shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The inversion hotspot has the longest stem structure for any of the theoretically predicted sites with a propensity to form ssDNA hairpins in the uGCR chrV L breakpoint region.
source: This hotspot, when present in ssDNA, is predicted to form a ssDNA hairpin with a 3 nt loop and a 15 bp stem (Figure 3B), which is the longest stem available for ssDNA hairpins in the uGCR assay breakpoint region (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 62 other ssDNA hairpin-forming sequences in the breakpoint region resulted in shorter stem structures ranging from 4 to 14 bp and were used less frequently.
source: In addition to the hotspot-mediated GCRs, we identified foldback inversions that were mediated by 62 other ssDNA hairpin-forming sequences present in the breakpoint region; however, these hairpin-forming sequences resulted in shorter stem structures ranging from 4 to 14 bp and were used less frequently (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: The sae2Δ hotspotΔ strain had an overall uGCR rate similar to the sae2Δ strain containing the hotspot.
source: The sae2Δ hotspotΔ strain had an overall uGCR rate and a foldback inversion GCR rate (9 of 12 GCRs were foldback inversions) that were similar to those of the sae2Δ strain containing the hotspot (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: None of the inversion sites used in GCRs isolated from the sae2Δ hotspotΔ strain were next to the deleted hotspot or were used more than once.
source: None of the inversion sites used in GCRs isolated from the sae2Δ hotspotΔ strain were next to the deleted hotspot or were used more than once (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The inversion hotspot does not induce DNA damage but redirects DNA damage into the formation of foldback inversion GCRs.
source: These results argue against a role of the hotspot in inducing DNA damage, but would be consistent with a role of the inversion hotspot in redirecting DNA damage present in a sae2Δ strain into the formation of foldback inversion GCRs mediated by the inversion hotspot.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from the hotspot deletion experiment.

claim: Induction of the centromeric DSB (chrV:34,470) places the hotspot sequence on the telomeric fragment where it cannot direct hairpin-mediated inversions oriented towards the centromere after resection.
source: Induction of the centromeric DSB (chrV:34,470) places the hotspot sequence on the telomeric fragment where it cannot direct hairpin-mediated inversions oriented towards the centromere after resection.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the position of the DSB relative to the hotspot.

claim: GCRs recovered from wild-type and sae2Δ uGCR strains after centromeric DSB induction did not involve the hotspot and were predominantly de novo telomere addition-mediated GCRs or microhomology-mediated translocations.
source: Consistent with this, the GCRs recovered from both the wild-type and sae2Δ uGCR strains did not involve the hotspot and were predominantly de novo telomere addition-mediated GCRs (11 of 24 GCRs) or microhomology-mediated translocations (11 of 24 GCRs) (Figure 4; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Cleavage at the telomeric DSB site (chrV:30,843) would allow resection and hotspot hairpin formation to generate centromere-oriented inversions.
source: In contrast, cleavage at the telomeric DSB site (chrV:30,843) would allow resection and hotspot hairpin formation to generate centromere-oriented inversions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the position of the DSB relative to the hotspot.

claim: GCRs recovered from the wild-type parental strain after telomeric DSB induction were predominantly de novo telomere addition-mediated GCRs (11 of 12 GCRs).
source: The GCRs recovered from the wild-type parental strain were predominantly de novo telomere addition-mediated GCRs (11 of 12 GCRs), whereas the GCRs recovered from the sae2Δ mutant were primarily foldback inversions (10 of 12 GCRs; Figure 4; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: GCRs recovered from the sae2Δ mutant after telomeric DSB induction were primarily foldback inversions (10 of 12 GCRs).
source: The GCRs recovered from the wild-type parental strain were predominantly de novo telomere addition-mediated GCRs (11 of 12 GCRs), whereas the GCRs recovered from the sae2Δ mutant were primarily foldback inversions (10 of 12 GCRs; Figure 4; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Only two of the foldback inversions recovered from the sae2Δ strain after telomeric DSB induction were mediated by the hotspot.
source: Remarkably, only two of the foldback inversions recovered from the sae2Δ strain in this case were mediated by the hotspot, and eight were mediated by another hairpin-forming sequence immediately adjacent to the cleavage site (coordinates chrV:30,857_30,872; predicted hairpin with a 6 bp stem) (Figure 4; Figure 2—source data 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Eight foldback inversions recovered from the sae2Δ strain after telomeric DSB induction were mediated by a hairpin-forming sequence immediately adjacent to the cleavage site with a predicted 6 bp stem.
source: Remarkably, only two of the foldback inversions recovered from the sae2Δ strain in this case were mediated by the hotspot, and eight were mediated by another hairpin-forming sequence immediately adjacent to the cleavage site (coordinates chrV:30,857_30,872; predicted hairpin with a 6 bp stem) (Figure 4; Figure 2—source data 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Short-stem hairpins primarily mediate inverted foldback formation when they are proximal to a DSB.
source: In addition, our analysis of CRISPR/Cas9-induced DSBs indicates that short-stemmed hairpins primarily mediate inverted foldback formation when they are proximal to a DSB, whereas long-stemmed hairpins can mediate inverted foldback formation when they are either proximal or distal to the DSB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Long-stemmed hairpins can mediate inverted foldback formation when they are either proximal or distal to the DSB.
source: In addition, our analysis of CRISPR/Cas9-induced DSBs indicates that short-stemmed hairpins primarily mediate inverted foldback formation when they are proximal to a DSB, whereas long-stemmed hairpins can mediate inverted foldback formation when they are either proximal or distal to the DSB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRISPR/Cas9 experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Foldback inversions observed tended to use hairpins within 50 bp of the DSB.
source: Analysis of potential hairpin-forming sequences centromeric to the induced DSBs suggested that foldback inversions observed tended to use hairpins within 50 bp of the DSB.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within 50 bp of the DSB, potential hairpins used in foldback inversions tended to have shorter loop lengths and longer stem lengths than those that were not used.
source: Within this 50 bp region, potential hairpins used in foldback inversions tended to have shorter loop lengths and longer stem lengths than those that were not used (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In GCRs isolated from strains with mre11 or sae2 defects, the predicted hairpin loop sizes were short (median of 4 and 3 nt, respectively).
source: Comparison of foldback inversions formed in strains with defects in MRE11 or SAE2 to those formed in strains with defects in TEL1, MRC1, and SWR1 revealed that two distinct classes of ssDNA hairpins mediate foldback inversions. In GCRs isolated from strains with mre11 or sae2 defects, the predicted hairpin loop sizes were short (median of 4 and 3 nt, respectively), whereas hairpins in GCRs isolated in strains with wild-type MRE11 and SAE2 had larger loops (median 36 nt), which could be many thousands of nucleotides in length (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Hairpins in GCRs isolated in strains with wild-type MRE11 and SAE2 had larger loops (median 36 nt), which could be many thousands of nucleotides in length.
source: Comparison of foldback inversions formed in strains with defects in MRE11 or SAE2 to those formed in strains with defects in TEL1, MRC1, and SWR1 revealed that two distinct classes of ssDNA hairpins mediate foldback inversions. In GCRs isolated from strains with mre11 or sae2 defects, the predicted hairpin loop sizes were short (median of 4 and 3 nt, respectively), whereas hairpins in GCRs isolated in strains with wild-type MRE11 and SAE2 had larger loops (median 36 nt), which could be many thousands of nucleotides in length (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The length of the hairpin stems observed did not appear to be influenced by the different GCR-inducing mutations tested.
source: In contrast to the effects on hairpin loop size, the length of the hairpin stems observed did not appear to be influenced by the different GCR-inducing mutations tested (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 10 foldback inversions selected in a tel1Δ single mutant were mediated by hairpins that often had large loops (median 26 nt, range 4 nt to 44 nt).
source: In a previous study, we found that the 10 foldback inversions selected in a tel1Δ single mutant (10 of 31 GCRs) were mediated by hairpins that often had large loops (median 26 nt, range 4 nt to 44 nt; Figure 6A; Putnam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and citation to Putnam et al., 2014.

claim: The inversion hotspot was not observed among the inversion sites that mediated the formation of foldback inversions in the tel1Δ mutant.
source: In addition, the inversion hotspot was not observed among the inversion sites that mediated the formation of foldback inversions in the tel1Δ mutant (Figure 3A; p=5×10−5, Fisher's exact test; Putnam et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Putnam et al., 2014.

claim: All GCRs selected in a sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant were foldback inversions mediated by small-loop hairpins (median 3 nt).
source: Therefore, we determined the structures of 11 GCRs selected in a sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant and found that all these GCRs were foldback inversions mediated by small-loop hairpins (median 3 nt; Figure 3A; Figure 6), and 8 of these were mediated by the inversion hotspot (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 6.

claim: 8 of 11 GCRs in the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant were mediated by the inversion hotspot.
source: Therefore, we determined the structures of 11 GCRs selected in a sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant and found that all these GCRs were foldback inversions mediated by small-loop hairpins (median 3 nt; Figure 3A; Figure 6), and 8 of these were mediated by the inversion hotspot (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effect of the sae2Δ mutation dominates the GCR spectrum in the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant.
source: Thus, the effect of the sae2Δ mutation dominates the GCR spectrum in the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant.

claim: Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2-Sae2 preferentially suppresses foldback inversions mediated by short-loop hairpins.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that: (1) Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2-Sae2 preferentially suppresses foldback inversions mediated by short-loop hairpins
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from multiple mutants.

claim: Foldback inversions formed in the presence of a functional Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2-Sae2 complex are primarily due to large-loop hairpins that escape surveillance by this complex.
source: (2) foldback inversions formed in the presence of a functional Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2-Sae2 complex, including those in mutants with increased rates of foldback inversion formation, are primarily due to large-loop hairpins that escape surveillance by this complex
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from multiple mutants.

claim: Short-loop hairpins may form at higher frequencies relative to large-loop hairpins.
source: (3) short-loop hairpins may form at higher frequencies relative to large-loop hairpins, as short-loop hairpins accumulate in mutants like the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant where both types of hairpins can form.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that short-loop hairpins dominate in the sae2Δ tel1Δ double mutant.

claim: Exo1 and Sgs1/Dna2 define the two major pathways mediating resection from DSBs.
source: Exo1 and Sgs1/Dna2 define the two major pathways mediating resection from DSBs (Gravel et al., 2008; Mimitou and Symington, 2008; Zhu et al., 2008
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gravel et al., 2008, Mimitou and Symington, 2008, and Zhu et al., 2008.

claim: The exo1Δ single mutant primarily accumulated de novo telomere addition GCRs (10 of 11 GCRs).
source: The exo1Δ single mutant primarily accumulated de novo telomere addition GCRs (10 of 11 GCRs; Figure 7)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant primarily accumulated short loop hairpin-mediated foldback inversion GCRs (16 of 18 GCRs).
source: whereas the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant primarily accumulated short loop hairpin-mediated foldback inversion GCRs (16 of 18 GCRs).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both the uGCR and foldback inversion GCR rates of the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant were ~20% of that of the sae2Δ single mutant.
source: Both the uGCR and foldback inversion GCR rates of the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant were ~20% of that of the sae2Δ single mutant (Figure 7A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The foldback inversions selected in the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant were primarily formed using the inversion hotspot (10 of 16).
source: The foldback inversions selected in the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant were primarily formed using the inversion hotspot (10 of 16; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in GCR rate and the altered GCR spectrum in the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant are consistent with the idea that Exo1 promotes resection to expose hairpin-forming sequences but is not absolutely required.
source: The reduction in GCR rate and the altered GCR spectrum in the sae2Δ exo1Δ double mutant are consistent with the idea that Exo1 promotes resection to expose hairpin-forming sequences but is not absolutely required for the resection necessary to generate foldback inversions in a sae2Δ mutant.

claim: Sgs1, like Exo1, promotes but is not absolutely required for resection leading to foldback inversion formation.

claim: Individual loss of Exo1 or Sgs1 modestly reduces the accumulation of hairpin-mediated GCRs in sae2Δ mutants.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from the sae2Δ mus81Δ double mutant.
